items.stem: One program must find an ID in 1,000 entries in no order. A second program must find an ID in 1,000 entries in ID order. Which is faster, and by how much?

options.text: The second program, which needs about 10 checks. The first may need all 1,000.
options.feedback: Halving 1,000 entries takes at most 10 guesses, because 1,000 is below 1,024. The unsorted list may need every entry.

options.text: The first program, because sorting is not needed for one search.
options.feedback: The second list is already sorted, so nobody has to sort it. That list gives the shorter search.

options.text: They take the same time, because both lists hold 1,000 entries.
options.feedback: The lists have the same size, but only the sorted list lets the program rule out half the entries per guess.

items.stem: You have learned that item C is larger than item F, and that item F is larger than item B. Do you need to compare C and B?

options.text: Yes, a comparison is the only way to know.
options.feedback: The first two results already settle it. Each result can be reused.

options.text: No, C must be larger than B.
options.feedback: If C is larger than F and F is larger than B, then C is larger than B. Sorting methods use this to skip comparisons.

options.text: Only if C and B end up next to each other.
options.feedback: The order of C and B follows from the first two results, wherever the items sit.

items.stem: A sorted list has 63 cells. Your first guess is the middle cell, and its ID is too high. How many cells are still open?

options.text: 62 cells, because only the guessed cell is ruled out.
options.feedback: Sorted order also rules out every cell on the high side of the guess.

options.text: 15 cells, because one guess halves the list twice.
options.feedback: One guess halves the list once.

options.text: 31 cells, because the guess and the whole high side are gone.
options.feedback: The middle cell leaves 31 cells on each side. The high side is gone, so 31 remain.

items.stem: A records app slows down badly when its student table grows from 10,000 to 1,000,000 rows. Searches by student ID read every row. Which change helps most?

options.text: Tell the users to search much less often than now.
options.feedback: Each search still reads every row, so fewer searches only hide the cost.

options.text: Add an index on the ID column, so searches halve.
options.feedback: An index keeps the IDs in order. A search then takes about 20 guesses for 1,000,000 rows.

options.text: Give the developer a faster laptop to run it on.
options.feedback: A faster machine reads each row sooner, but the work still grows with every row added.
